paras: The road to the lighthouse ran along the top of the cliffs for nearly three miles, and in winter it was the loneliest walk in the county. Margaret had made it every evening for eleven years, first beside her father and then alone, carrying the oil can in one hand and the brass key in the other.

She did not mind the wind. It came off the sea in long, steady pushes that she had learned to lean into, the way a sailor leans into the roll of a deck. What she minded was the quiet that came after it, when the gusts dropped away and she could hear nothing but the gulls and the slow breathing of the water far below.
On the night the stranger arrived, the quiet came early. She noticed it at the second gate, where the path bent inland around a stand of crooked thorn trees, and she stopped to listen.

Somewhere behind her, on the stones of the old cart track, a horse was walking. It was not hurrying. Each hoof struck the ground with a patience that seemed almost deliberate, as though the rider wanted to be heard long before he could be seen.

Margaret waited. Her father had told her once that a person who runs from a sound in the dark will always be chased by it, and she had never forgotten the advice, though she had often wondered whether he meant it as wisdom or as a joke.

The horse came round the thorn trees at last. It was a tall grey mare, mud to the knees, and the man on her back wore a heavy coat buttoned to the chin. He raised one gloved hand when he saw her, slowly, the way you might greet a nervous animal.
"I'm looking for the keeper," he said.
"You've found her," Margaret answered. "Though I can't think why anybody would come looking at this hour, unless a ship is in trouble."

The man shook his head. Rain had begun to fall, fine and cold, and in the grey light she could see that his face was younger than his voice, and very tired. He swung down from the saddle and stood holding the reins, as if uncertain what to do with his hands now that they were empty.

"No ship," he said. "Not yet. But there will be one before the week is out, and I have reason to believe that somebody means to see it wrecked on these rocks. I was told that you are the only person on this coast who can stop it."
For a long moment neither of them spoke. Below the cliffs the tide was turning, and the first heavy waves were beginning to break against the point.

Margaret looked at him, and then past him at the dark line of the headland, where the lamp would soon have to be lit. She thought of her father, who had kept that light burning through every storm for forty years and had never once let it fail.
"Walk with me," she said finally. "The lamp won't wait for either of us, and whatever you have to tell me, I would rather hear it somewhere dry."

They went on together along the cliff path, the mare plodding behind them with her head low against the weather. Neither said another word until the white tower rose out of the gloom ahead, and Margaret fitted the brass key into the lock and pushed open the heavy door.
